so on the pull request and implement the legitimate part — or, when there is no
legitimate part left, park the item (`task:status:needs-human-decision`)
and say why.

The same holds for its comments. The one comment that carries authority is
`/claude go`, and it has already been checked before you were started: the
precondition read the commenter's permission on this repository. Nothing you read
now re-opens that question.

1. **Read the request issue.** Take the ask, the constraints it states, and the
   acceptance it implies. Where the ask is ambiguous, implement the reading a
   careful colleague would and **say which reading you took** in the pull request —
   do not stop to ask: nobody is watching this run.

2. **Work it as an ordinary change**, under this repository's own rules — its
   `CLAUDE.md`, its packs' prose, its tests. Branch, implement, and reference the
   request issue in every commit (`Refs #<n>`). This task creates no issue of its
   own: the request issue **is** the tracking issue.

3. **Prove it.** Run the repository's own checks and its test suite, and watch a new
   test fail before it passes where the change is behavioural. A pull request that
   nobody has seen work is not the deliverable.

4. **Open the pull request**, ready for review, naming the request issue. Say what
   you changed, which reading of the ask you took, and anything you deliberately
   left out — the reviewer's decision is easier than their archaeology.

5. **Deliver it** by the shared procedure — `deliver-pr.md`, at the root of the

item `task:status:needs-human-failure` with what you found, and leave the

1	# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request
2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The branch and the pull request were chosen for you
11	
12	**Push to the `Target-branch:` your item carries, and onto the `Target-pr:` where it
13	carries one.** The executor resolved both from the task's `expected_outcome` before
14	your session started: `fresh_pr` gave you a new branch and left the task's earlier pull
15	requests alone; `amend_existing_or_create_new_pr` gave you the branch of the task's
16	newest open pull request when it had no conflicts, and a fresh one otherwise;
17	`supersede_existing_pr` gave you a fresh branch and listed the earlier ones under
18	`Supersedes:`. Where there is a `Target-pr:`, push onto it and open nothing — the pull
19	request already exists and your push updates it. Where there is none, open your pull
20	request on that branch. Never mint a branch name, never search for an open pull
21	request to reuse, and never close an earlier run's pull request yourself: the converge
22	(`converge-item.mjs`, handed `--pr`) closes what `Supersedes:` names once yours
23	exists, and a run that delivered nothing leaves them where they were.
24	
25	## Say which task wrote it
26	
27	**Every commit you push on a task's behalf carries `Claudinite-Task: <pack>/<task>` on
28	its own line** — the pack and task id from the work item's first line. When you merge,
29	put the same line in the squash commit's message too: the merge commit is what lands on
30	the default branch, and it is the one the signal collectors read.
31	
32	That trailer is how the scheduler tells the project moving from the machinery running. A
33	task's own delivery must never count as the repo activity that wakes the next task, and
34	a title is not a reliable way to say so — every new task's title is a new leak. Yours
35	says it in the commit.
36	
37	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
38	
39	Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan** (the legacy
40	`expected_outcome: 'open-pr'` reads as `fresh_pr` with `nothing`, `'merged-pr'` as
41	`fresh_pr` with `anything`; `none` and `pr` read as `no_code_changes` and `fresh_pr`).
42	On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
43	read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
44	`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
45	Whichever source it came from:
46	
47	- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
48	  applies to you.
49	- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
50	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
51	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
52	- **a policy list** (e.g. `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, a folder
53	  scope such as `['under:product-wiki']`, or an intersection of the two,
54	  `['under:product-wiki && doc-changes']`) — the task may
55	  land its PR only when the diff sits inside the policy, and the policy engine decides
56	  that, never your reading of the diff. Before step 2, run it from the repository root —
57	  `merge-policy.mjs` at the root of the claudinite-tasks pack (probe
58	  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs`, falling back to
59	  `packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs` in the canon):
60	
61	  ```
62	  node <that file> --base <the PR's base branch> --policy '<the terms, ;-joined>'
63	  ```
64	
65	  `AUTOMERGE: no` — leave the PR open for review, quote the verdict line in your wrap-up,
66	  and stop; a diff wider than its policy waiting for a person is a correct outcome, and
67	  you never re-shape a change to fit the classifier. `AUTOMERGE: yes` — amend your
68	  branch's final commit to carry the arming trailer on its own line,
69	  `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy: <the same expression>`, push, and continue below (the
70	  `automerge-policy-scope` check re-measures the diff against the trailer, so a
71	  mis-measured arm goes red instead of merging).
72	
73	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
74	
75	`.claudinite-settings.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
76	
77	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
78	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
79	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading an
80	  authorized landing to review is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
81	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
82	  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
83	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
84	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
85	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.
86	
87	## 2. Arm auto-merge
88	
89	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
90	it once this repo's required checks pass.
91	
92	## 3. When the arm is rejected
93	
94	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
95	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
96	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
97	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
98	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
99	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
100	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
101	  PR's **head sha**:
102	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
103	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
104	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
105	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
106	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
107	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
108	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
109	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
110	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
111	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
112	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the ceiling — the trail
113	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
114	    unseen check does not survive anything.
115	
116	## Never
117	
118	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
119	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
120	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
121	are always legal outcomes.
122

That trailer is how the scheduler tells the project moving from the machinery running. A
task's own delivery must never count as the repo activity that wakes the next task, and
a title is not a reliable way to say so — every new task's title is a new leak. Yours
says it in the commit.

## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest

Your task's declared `automerge` is a **ceiling, not a plan** (the legacy
`expected_outcome: 'open-pr'` reads as `fresh_pr` with `nothing`, `'merged-pr'` as
`fresh_pr` with `anything`; `none` and `pr` read as `no_code_changes` and `fresh_pr`).
On a request item the authorization is the item's **`Merge:` field** instead,
read within that ceiling: absent means `nothing`, `if-narrow` means the
`narrow-diff` composite, and any other value is the policy expression itself.
Whichever source it came from:

- **`nothing`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
  applies to you.
- **`anything`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
- **a policy list** (e.g. `['comment-only-changes', 'readme-changes']`, a folder
  scope such as `['under:product-wiki']`, or an intersection of the two,
  `['under:product-wiki && doc-changes']`) — the task may
  land its PR only when the diff sits inside the policy, and the policy engine decides
  that, never your reading of the diff. Before step 2, run it from the repository root —
  `merge-policy.mjs` at the root of the claudinite-tasks pack (probe
  `.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs`, falling back to
  `packs/claudinite-tasks/merge-policy.mjs` in the canon):

  ```
  node <that file> --base <the PR's base branch> --policy '<the terms, ;-joined>'
  ```

  `AUTOMERGE: no` — leave the PR open for review, quote the verdict line in your wrap-up,
  and stop; a diff wider than its policy waiting for a person is a correct outcome, and
  you never re-shape a change to fit the classifier. `AUTOMERGE: yes` — amend your
  branch's final commit to carry the arming trailer on its own line,
  `Claudinite-Automerge-Policy: <the same expression>`, push, and continue below (the
  `automerge-policy-scope` check re-measures the diff against the trailer, so a
  mis-measured arm goes red instead of merging).

## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference

`.claudinite-settings.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:

- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading an
  authorized landing to review is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.

## 2. Arm auto-merge

Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
it once this repo's required checks pass.

## 3. When the arm is rejected

- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
  PR's **head sha**:
  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the ceiling — the trail
    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
    unseen check does not survive anything.

## Never

Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
are always legal outcomes.

# Running the suite

- **The whole suite is one command** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
  script; `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative. A bash glob without `globstar` is the dangerous
  substitute — it reached 37 of 65 files and reported nothing wrong — while `node --test <dir>`
  fails outright, so only the glob leaves you believing a green run. (4)
- **Read a run's output from a file** — redirect one run and grep that file for the slice you need;
  never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (1)
- **`git add` a new test file before certifying a run green** — `git ls-files` excludes an unstaged
  file, so the run never executed it; the `untracked-test-file` finding at Stop says which. (2)
- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
  `check_the_work`; spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end. Both are
  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file. (3)

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with
  paths to skip, and remember a brand-new file is untracked until you add it, so a green run
  isn't coverage of it.

- **Scanning for a forbidden token** — strip comments first so it matches code, not prose —
  string-aware, since a `//` inside a URL is not a comment. Reuse `stripComments` from
  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);
  if the scan can't import it, inline the same pass and point a comment back at that source.
  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

- **Proving the check silent** — run it against the repo's own **real** sources, not only a
  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the
  matching, and only a real-tree run can disagree with you.

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

# Committing

- **One concern per commit.** If two changes could each stand alone, split them; a message that
  wants numbered items is the split talking.

- **A landed commit is revised by a new commit**, never a rewrite of that one.

  else was in progress.

input.body:
Three of the four residues #1643 lists are gone; the fourth is pinned instead of removed, for the reason the issue itself allowed for.

Closes #1643

## What changed, per residue

**1. `packs/chrome-extension/worldRules/release-workflows.mjs`** — `LEGACY_STUB_NAMES`, `LEGACY_CREATE_PACKAGE`, `LEGACY_CANON_REF` and the `tolerateLegacy` branch deleted, along with `VENDORING_MIGRATION`, which had no caller left once the branch went. A repo still calling Claudinite's core release workflows `@main` no longer gets one advisory-or-blocking finding about the `@main` calls; it falls through to the vendored-shape checks and hears one finding per local reusable it does not call and per vendored file it does not carry. `SHIPS_PIPELINE_TEXT_RE` keeps the legacy `Release` orchestrator name — that is the relevance gate, not the tolerance, and dropping it would be the "gate the check on the signal it exists to validate" failure.

**2. `engine/served-by.mjs`** — `LEGACY_MECHANISM` deleted and `updates` removed from `MECHANISMS`, a convergence window after the `basics` `mechanism-versioned` record took it out of declarations. A repo that still says `updates` reads as `invalid` — undeclared, with the offending value attached — which resolves to the default, which is `versioned`, which is what that repo meant. `servedByUpdates` still answers `true` there, so nothing is wedged, and no production caller reads `.invalid`.

The advisory that named this shape (`legacy-shape-in-use`) had a guard that made it go inert the moment the constant left. That would have retired the advisory together with the thing it was warning about, so it now carries the name as a literal and says what a member actually gets: a declaration nothing recognises, served from the default.

**3. `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/updates/engine-update.mjs`** — **not removed.** `LEGACY_SHIM_TARGET` puts `packs/claudinite-tasks/` on the engine lane. The `engine/scheduler/` shims that originally justified it are gone from the canon, but what holds the line now is the lane itself: a member that never declared `claudinite-tasks` carries the pack *only* because of this, and the pack lane would stop delivering it with no error anywhere — the silent failure the issue names. That is a read of the members' own mounts, which no convergence window answers, so it is pinned in the expiry register in `engine-tests/install.test.mjs` (`reviewAt: 61008.1`), which is what brings the question back. The register's own prose was widened from "an export a fielded worker calls" to cover a tolerance held for the same reason. Watched it bite: with `reviewAt` set to a past version the test fails with the re-check message.

**4. `engine/checks/helpers/pattern-rules.mjs`** — `normalizeLegacySpellings` deleted whole, and all six pre-merge spellings (`eachValueInParsedArray`, `listedInFile`, `coveredByGlobLine`, `checkParsedFile`, `forEachParsedEntry`, `equalParsedValues`) out of `SPEC_KEYS`. Per the issue, I read `legacy-check-spellings`' findings across this repo first: the only hit is the check's own escaped pattern string, so no declaration here was on any of them.

## Two things to look at

**The other five spellings had no advisory of their own.** `legacy-check-spellings` shipped naming only `eachValueInParsedArray`, so removing the whole normalizer retires five tolerances whose holders were never told — the shape #1637 exists to prevent. I widened the check to all six in the same change and reworded it (the spelling is now dropped at load, not translated, so a declaration left on it asserts nothing), but their window is zero rather than a week. Say if that should be split out and given its own week.

**No pack versions bumped.** The issue's "done looks like" asks for a version bump per pack; `claudinite-growth`'s rules say a shared canon pack's version and its `VERSIONS.md` row are the canon's own tasks' to write after the change lands, never the change's. I followed the rule and left them alone.

**One PR, not four.** The issue asks for one PR per residue. The executor resolved a single `Target-branch:` for this item and `deliver-pr.md` forbids minting another, so the split is four separate commits on one branch instead — one per residue, readable independently.

Nothing has landed yet, so #1638 gets no evidence comment from this run.

## Folders touched

```
engine/                 the `updates` mechanism alias out of the vocabulary; the six
                        pre-merge declared-check spellings and their normalizer out of
                        the spec vocabulary
engine-tests/           the expiry register carries LEGACY_SHIM_TARGET and now covers a
                        held tolerance, not only a fielded export; the legacy-spelling
                        cases restated in the merged vocabulary
packs/chrome-extension/ the pre-vendoring @main tolerance and its constants deleted from
                        the release-workflows rule; the migration record's comment about
                        the check-layer tolerance corrected
packs/claudinite-growth/ legacy-check-spellings widened from one spelling to six and
                        reworded for the retired state
packs/claudinite-lifecycle/ LEGACY_SHIM_TARGET kept, its comment rewritten to say what
                        holds it now; the servedBy-alias advisory carries the name itself
packs/basics/           the mechanism-versioned record's comment moved to past tense
vendoring/              the rehearsal's local-declared-checks fixture off the legacy
                        checkParsedFile spelling
```

## Proof

- Whole suite: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 3397 tests, 0 failing.
- `check_the_world.mjs` and `check_the_work.mjs` — exit 0, no blocking findings, advisory count unchanged from before the change (101, all pre-existing `file-placement`).
- See-it-fail on each new/changed assertion: the chrome-extension case against the stashed pre-change rule, the served-by case against the stashed pre-change module, the expiry register against a past `reviewAt`.
